podcasts.name: No Priors
podcasts.title: Taking on ServiceNow: Coding Agents the Rest of Us with Serval Co-Founder and CEO Jake Stauch
podcasts.transcript:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:09
This is the ultimate moonshot in enterprise software. These agents that go off and do work for you and magically discover all your problems and solve all your problems. And I think no one's really figured out how to do this well.

Speaker 2 | 00:09 - 00:13
This is kind of the OpenAI hugging face incidents or other things where agents are given a task and then

Speaker 1 | 00:13 - 00:28
they do something that's unexpected. The agent becomes pretty competent. They could theoretically just start writing code that could take action on all your systems, and that is an unbounded security risk that I don't think anyone's gonna be able to take anytime soon. On the one hand, you want these to be very autonomous without somebody babysitting babysitting them. Them.

Speaker 1 | 00:28 - 00:40
On the other hand, autonomy is very scary in the enterprise. Serval is the boundary. Serval is the guardrails. We are the way that a large enterprise with a lot of rules and approvals and process and politics can adopt these tools safely and comfortably at scale.

Speaker 3 | 00:48 - 01:08
Hi, listeners. Welcome back to No Priors. Today, Elad and I are here with Jake Stouch, cofounder and CEO of Serval. Serval, with all the speed of the African wildcat, is trying to attack ServiceNow and more broadly bringing the power of cogeneration to IT and enterprise teams overall. Welcome, Jake.

Speaker 2 | 01:08 - 01:10
Jake, thanks for joining us today on Enterprise.

Speaker 1 | 01:10 - 01:13
Thank you. Great to be here. Maybe you could tell us a

Speaker 2 | 01:13 - 01:18
little bit more about your history and how you started Serval, and what what is the problem that you started with, or why did start working on this to begin with?

Speaker 1 | 01:18 - 01:31
Yeah. So background, Serval is enterprise automation, enterprise service management. The idea is you can ask questions and get help at work and automate a lot of the parts of the job you don't enjoy, and we do that through cogen agents. So that's the... What the company does.

Speaker 1 | 01:31 - 02:04
We compete with companies like ServiceNow, is historically the big legacy provider in the space. I discovered this category actually working at a previous company called Verkada, where we sold enterprise physical security products to IT teams, spent many, many years talking to IT teams, figuring out what to build for them. And one of the things I love to to do with these teams is ask them, what do you spend the most money on, and what do you hate the most? And ServiceNow would top a lot of those lists. And so I was always interested in this category of maybe there's a better solution here, but it wasn't clear for most of my time there how you'd ever beat ServiceNow.

Speaker 1 | 02:04 - 02:10
They're a great company. They've done so much so well, and why would you be able to compete with them?

Speaker 3 | 02:10 - 02:12
What was frustrating for users about it?

Speaker 1 | 02:13 - 02:49
I think so hard to build in the platform. So it's a very robust, customizable, powerful platform that can map to all these enterprise workflows fundamentally. It's a workflow automation platform, and so it can do so much, but every idea you have for doing something cool, you have to go and implement, and a lot times you're bringing consultants to implement it. So it's always kind of running six to twelve months behind where you want it to be, and it's fine if you're building something that's gonna last five, ten years, like a big onboarding flow, and nothing about your business is gonna change, so you can invest all that upfront effort, and then it gets deployed, and it works for a while. But for just trying to keep up with all the automation that you wanna build, ServiceNow is not able to catch up.

Speaker 1 | 02:49 - 02:59
And and then it's very expensive, and it keeps getting more expensive over time, so that frustration of it's not keeping up with where I wanna go as a business, and it keeps getting more expensive, that's what was driving a lot of the frustration.

Speaker 2 | 02:59 - 03:32
I think one thing that you mentioned that's really interesting about what you do is if you look at the world of AI adoption, a lot of the really early adoption is coding agents. Yes. And that's engineers using it to build applications for their business, for products, other things. And what you folks have been doing is really pioneering expansion of the category in terms of saying, We should let anybody internally, an IT person, etcetera, build internal products or tools that can be used broadly across the enterprise. You're basically providing coding agents for all the internal stuff for people who often aren't that adept at coding.

Speaker 1 | 03:32 - 03:32
So can

Speaker 2 | 03:32 - 03:34
you talk more about that? Think it's super fascinating. Yeah.

Speaker 1 | 03:34 - 04:06
Love this idea of coding agents for the rest of us, because we think so much of the early enterprise adoption in AI has been engineering teams. And if you think about why that is, there's a lot of reasons. Obviously, early adopters and a lot of different technologies, but also they're able to build and experiment with these tools because they have this process of code review. It's very safe for even a 19 year old intern to build something very powerful and then go through this process before it goes into production. We wanna bring that same capability to the rest of the enterprise, so we build a platform that brings coding agents to IT departments who then can bring it to HR and finance and people teams and legal teams.

Speaker 1 | 04:06 - 04:25
And they can do it because under the hood, it's coding agents, but then you have all these abstractions and guardrails and controls. So things go through approval. They go through a staging and, approval cycle and audit trail and all of that. And so it's how do you build a system that makes it easy for everyone to be a builder. And the core insight here was that IT actually wants to build stuff.

Speaker 1 | 04:25 - 04:41
And for most of the world, they don't have an engineering department. They have an IT department. Most companies have an IT department, not not a a team of software engineers. And so IT is what's building and configuring technology for the company, and we are building essentially the AI platform for them. How does how does that

Speaker 2 | 04:41 - 04:51
run into things like all the different more, like, workforce agents that are being developed, like Dot from OpenAI or, you know, some of these things where you almost have a virtual assistant that will go and do things for you?

Speaker 1 | 04:51 - 05:17
Yeah. Think those really work well for consumers and SMB and even a lot of the mid market organizations. In a large enterprise, there's so much, and I didn't even really appreciate this going in. There is so much process around approvals, around what you can and can't do. The permission sets of any individual are so limited that even if you were allowed to bring your agent to work, which a lot of cases you're not, what it can what it can do is so incredibly limited.

Speaker 1 | 05:17 - 05:59
It can it can barely even read your emails. And so when you think about all the stuff you need to do at work and all the systems you wanna touch and all the interesting automations you could build, your personal permissions end up being so limited that these personal agents are also incredibly limited and all... Not all that useful. So what we can do, because we work with these IT teams that can connect with, you know, service account credentials and admin level permissions, we can create a structure where people can access elevated permissions and do all these crazy things in the org, but with very, very strict deterministic approval cycles, workflows that are deterministic, and an audit trail, because under the hood, we are also a ticketing system. So you say, okay, I want my agent to go do x, y, and z.

Speaker 1 | 06:00 - 06:29
Well, most organizations are gonna be very uncomfortable with that at the large enterprise scale. But with Servo, that's gonna create access requests that go through an approval process, and all of that's gonna be documented and logged, and then you can get just in time access to be able to run that deterministic workflow one time, and all of it's gonna be tracked. And, yes, it's a little bit more annoying than the magical personal agent experience we love with Instinct and Muse and all these tools, but it's what has to be true for a large enterprise, especially a regulated enterprise, to ever adopt these kinds of technologies.

Speaker 2 | 06:29 - 06:51
And this also, I guess, feeds into the traditional diffusion of this technology, which has been consulting firms, the Accenture's and Deloitte's and the like of the world kind of owning a piece of this, doing the implementation for people. You're kind of taking that and putting it in the hands directly of the IT department. Are you also exploring this Mooresburg sort of forward deployed motion, or how do you actually get this really built out in the enterprise or used effectively?

Speaker 1 | 06:51 - 07:04
Yeah. Absolutely. Diffusion is obviously the gap here. The technology can do so much, and and enterprises have barely scratched the surface of what's possible. And a lot of that is just understanding the people, the process, what workflows actually exist, how you want them to exist in the future.

Speaker 1 | 07:04 - 07:55
And we think that you still need people for that. So we deploy both a a deployment strategist, we call them, and a deployed software engineer that go on-site with customers, figure out how do we implement this, how do we solve all your problems as a business, and then walk you through the implementation. What we found though is that a lot of times, after we've got this implemented and deployed, customers then have a long tail of more stuff they want. And and as we've discovered with software engineering, there's actually unlimited demand for work, and we've started to build out a team. We call it ProServal, or or automation engineering is is the field, and we bring in these automation engineers to kind of do ongoing continued support and services because there's so much that they want to automate, and they need the help to be able to figure out what can be automated, what do the processes look like, how do we navigate all of our systems, and then put it into production with a product like Serval.

Speaker 3 | 07:55 - 07:57
How old is the company today?

Speaker 1 | 07:58 - 07:59
Two and a half years.

Speaker 3 | 07:59 - 08:17
And, you know, if you just look at ServiceNow as a business, I feel like Serval's one of the only companies that is like, we are direct attack replacing enterprise systems of record, including for large enterprises. At the beginning, did you think you were going to do that? Like, do you... How do you eat the elephant? Yes.

Speaker 3 | 08:17 - 08:20
Just in terms of, you know, how big that product suite is.

Speaker 1 | 08:20 - 08:39
I like to say everything has gone exactly according to our very delusional plans. So we set out from the beginning to be the largest enterprise software company of all time. We actually made a list of all the companies. We circled ServiceNow, and we said we're gonna beat them, and we're gonna build something much bigger. We said that on day one, when it was two people in my cofounder Alex's living room, and we just said we're gonna do it.

Speaker 1 | 08:39 - 08:45
And so even though that was crazy, that was always the intention. We didn't grow into that ambition. We set out from the beginning. I think that that actually

Speaker 3 | 08:45 - 08:50
A lot of people would have started with, like, you know, automation on top of their ticketing system,

Speaker 1 | 08:50 - 09:00
for example. Yeah. So the the way you typically go after these these large enterprise startups, at least, they they build, like, the layer Mhmm. Or they go down market. And those are kind of the two common approaches.

Speaker 1 | 09:00 - 09:06
Let's build a small layer, play nice with the big incumbents, AI agent on top of Salesforce, which, like, you know, it's it really caps out.

Speaker 2 | 09:06 - 09:14
Maybe the only one that worked is Veeva or something. Right? Because they... They'd started off on Salesforce, and then they migrated to become their own platform. So they're they're the only one that I can think of that backwards integrated.

Speaker 1 | 09:14 - 09:23
It's really tough. It, like, caps you unless you find some niche to kind of, like, expand into later on. The other approach is we just go down mark. You know? Go down market, service the SMB and mid market.

Speaker 1 | 09:23 - 09:29
And you see that with a lot of, you know, competitors to Workday, competitors to Salesforce. They just say, we're gonna be that, but for the lower end. And we just looked

Speaker 3 | 09:29 - 09:31
This is rippling or HubSpot Exactly. For the first ten

Speaker 1 | 09:31 - 09:45
years. Exactly. And we looked at that, we said, why not just go after the big one? It's it's much harder, but at least the prize is quite big if you win. And I think that was so important for us, because you end up making so many different decisions if you're building for a large enterprise from day one.

Speaker 1 | 09:45 - 09:53
All the product decisions, how you build your team, how you think about growth, they're fundamentally different than if you go and you serve one market, then you hope to expand later on.

Speaker 2 | 09:53 - 09:55
How'd you choose this versus Salesforce server? You know,

Speaker 1 | 09:55 - 10:38
there's a few other sort of canonical giant companies in different categories. I think we didn't really understand how we'd beat the other companies, and why we had an advantage, and what what AI unlocked that they couldn't catch up to. And what we understood about ServiceNow because of our experience with IT is that fundamentally, it is a workflow automation platform. And our belief, me and my cofounder, and my cofounder really had this this idea early on that code was the right way to express automation in the enterprise, that you should just build all automations in code, and these drag and drop workflow builders is a painful level of abstraction because it's too complex for nontechnical users, and it's annoyingly abstracted for technical users. Code is a better way of building automations.

Speaker 1 | 10:38 - 11:02
The problem, obviously, is not many people can write code and and do it quickly enough for it to make sense for automation. And so as AI made this possible, that was what it clicked for both of us, that actually, if code is the right way to build automation and now anyone can write code, we can build a better automation platform. And what is an automation platform is actually... What is the best market for an automation platform? It's actually taking on these massive legacy software companies like ServiceNow.

Speaker 2 | 11:02 - 11:08
I guess two and a half years ago when you got started, though, most of the coding stuff was sort of tab complete. It did not work. Yeah. And so To

Speaker 1 | 11:08 - 11:13
be very clear, like, this is a this is a brilliant idea. Yeah. But in practice, when we started building this Yeah.

Speaker 2 | 11:14 - 11:22
What was the assumption? Was it that the the coding would get much better? Was it that you'd build tooling and that you didn't need to because things got so good? I'm sort of curious of that transition.

Speaker 1 | 11:22 - 11:51
The bet was that coding agents would be... Would get very good. And the theory there was it's a verifiable domain, and and it should actually hill climb fairly well. And so we believed fundamentally that coding agents would get good, at least for these very... I didn't expect them to get as good as they are for just general purpose software development, but for deterministic procedural scripts of reset password, get approval, like, all of these things are just so defined and verifiable that we felt like it would get good at those things.

Speaker 1 | 11:52 - 12:12
And so from a workflow automation perspective, we thought it would get there. In the early days, it did not. So what we ended up doing in all our early demos, we would prompt the LLM and say, hey. Here's a suggested way you might wanna build a password reset workflow. And so we'd we'd we'd seed it with, like, a lot of examples, and then over time, we'd make that library bigger and bigger.

Speaker 1 | 12:12 - 12:21
But then the models just got so good that eventually, it became hard to break. It became hard for you to give workflow that it couldn't automate if the APIs existed. Yeah.

Speaker 3 | 12:21 - 12:36
When you think about where coding agents are today and what your customers want, like, what are you... Are you and Alex excited about them getting better from here? Are you nervous? Like, what do you think it looks like in terms of impact on your own product?

Speaker 1 | 12:36 - 13:01
We are so excited for them to get better because I think it unlocks a lot of the things that we'd love to do around, you know, better browser use and computer use and more of a approach to background agents and personal agents that can be really useful in the enterprise. We're excited for the evolution of the category. We've always believed fundamentally that we are not building the LLMs ourselves. We are building the guardrails. We are building the the boundaries.

Speaker 1 | 13:02 - 13:31
And the boundaries are the product for us, because we are the way that a large enterprise, with a lot of rules and approvals and process and politics, can adopt these tools safely and comfortably at scale. And so SERVL is the boundary. SERVL is the guardrails. The intelligence getting better just makes our product more powerful, and also makes our customers wanna actually clamp down even further on those boundaries, on those guardrails. And I actually think access is going to get more and more controlled for individuals in the enterprise.

Speaker 1 | 13:32 - 13:39
And as access becomes stricter, and you let people do less and less and your permissions get more and more narrow, which I think is going to happen

Speaker 3 | 13:39 - 13:40
Why is it gonna happen?

Speaker 1 | 13:40 - 13:47
Because I think if if you think about... You know, I might safely give you more permissions than you need because I don't actually think you're gonna do all that much damage.

Speaker 3 | 13:47 - 13:47
Uh-huh.

Speaker 1 | 13:47 - 13:58
But if you have access to all these agents, then the damage you can do with any kind of, like, slightly elevated beyond normal permissions expands. And and we're seeing this in cybersecurity risk right now.

Speaker 3 | 13:58 - 13:59
Absolutely.

Speaker 1 | 13:59 - 14:31
And and so what I'm actually gonna wanna do if I'm a large enterprise is shrink everyone's permissions down to truly least privilege. Like, you cannot access any document, and you cannot take any action unless you absolutely need to do it for your job. But then you're going to have exceptions all the time. We are the layer that grants those exceptions and makes it possible for you to set up approval procedures around that, have an audit trail and a ticket associated with that. So by owning how privileges get escalated in the enterprise, we actually become more powerful and more essential the more you clamp down on end user permissions.

Speaker 3 | 14:31 - 14:47
Is there, like, a story or a win you can share as to... You know, people would be taking a big risk going with you to replace a very embedded incumbent. Right? It's a investment of their own time. I assume it's, like, personal risk.

Speaker 3 | 14:47 - 14:52
Like, why do that, or is there is there an experience where people have already gone through to the other side?

Speaker 1 | 14:52 - 15:10
I think we have to convince ourselves and our customers that Serval is the way you get promoted at work. And this is top down. Right?

Top down. So we sell into the C level across the IT leadership in in many cases, then distribute into other departments. And that is the message is this is... People built their career on ServiceNow. You're gonna build your career on this next generation, and we're seeing this play out.

So one of our largest customers is Fox. Fox Corporation adopted Servo company wide, and the person who led that migration on ground level actually got nominated to be the MVP of the entire company. Wow. And and got an award for his work there, and that is really what we're about, is we're convincing our customers, saying, like, this is the way to not just prove that you're you're useful to your organization, but to prove that you might be the most essential person to your company because you're leading this change. And we're so pivotable...

Pivotal to the AI transformation story that I think it's a... It's something we can sell really nicely to our customers.

Speaker 2 | 15:59 - 16:10
When you started Serval, I think you were very, adept at thinking ahead. Right? So you knew coding agents or coding would get better. You knew there was this way of transformation. You kind of identified the good market segment to go after.
